chapter_theme: At the wedding of Civakan and his uncle Govindan's daughter Ilakkanai, the attendants praise the bride and the rival kings burn with envy; the priests kindle the fire and Civakan takes the gift-water and circles the fire; the women prepare the bridal bed, and the night is told in the figure of a rain-cloud filling a tank.

cast.role: Govindan's daughter, the bride; never named in the verses of this run
the bride's father, Civakan's maternal uncle, king of Videha
the women of the wedding hall who attend the bride and make the bridal bed
the umbrella kings who watch the wedding, some of them losing suitors
the nurses who brought up the bride
the priests who kindle the wedding fire
the fire god, who rises from the sacrificial fire

2453.reading: A string of loving names (sugar-cane, honey, nectar, jewelled vina, swan, peahen, koel, doe) is poured on the king's daughter, addressed as the doll of the jewel-wearing king.
2453.nuance: The verse names no speaker; the women of the wedding hall are taken as the speakers from the verses that follow, and 'the king's doll' is Govindan's daughter by the chapter's title.

2454.reading: The bride steps aside while her attendants cry that they will lay down a bed softer than anicham flowers and swan down, which she would not tread for fear of its heat, and praise her feet.
2454.nuance: The syntax of lines 2 to 4 is hard (whose feet are praised, and who lays what); the reading follows the plain order of the words.
2454.event: The bride, praised by her attendants, steps aside from a flower-soft path.

2455.reading: The bride comes into the cool wedding pavilion, with a thousand gold pillars and a hundred gem pillars and wreaths of flowers, like a daughter of the celestials.
2455.event: The bride arrives at the pavilion.

2456.reading: Seeing the form of the king's daughter, whose moon-face and doe-like grace outdo Kaman's bow and arrows, the umbrella kings are scorched in the eyes as by fire and cannot rest.
2456.nuance: The kings' pain is the pain of the losing suitors; it makes the bride's worth the measure of what Civakan wins.
2456.event: The assembled kings, seeing the bride, burn with longing and grief.

2457.reading: The nurses who reared the bride, seeing her eyes as Death that drinks lives, pull out the cord and show it, and the verse closes with a wish that evil be across the whole sea-ringed land.
2457.nuance: The lines on the nurses' act and the word உத்தராசங்கம் are obscure; the verse closes with the same refrain as 2466 and may be a ward against the evil eye, which the Tamil does not state.
2457.event: The bride's nurses show a cord at the sight of her death-dealing eyes.

2458.reading: The onlookers say that today they saw Death with their own eyes: it is the great wide eyes of a woman with a waist like an elephant cow's, whose breasts no praise can describe.
2458.nuance: No speaker is named; the kings of 2456 and 2459 are taken, though any watcher could be meant.

2459.reading: The kings, seeing the bride's soft reddened feet, say that Civakan, on whose head-tuft she will tread with sounding anklets, must have done penance, which they themselves could not bear, and fall into grief.
2459.nuance: The kings give the win to Civakan's earlier tavam, which the verse does not specify; the Jain epic lets the losers name deeds as the cause of his luck.
2459.event: The rival kings lament that Civakan has won the bride.

claims.claim: a man wins a rare bride by penance done earlier

2460.reading: The nectar river of the bride flows down from the golden mountain Govindan toward the coral sea that is Civakan, but sinks into the pond of the sacrificial hall.
2460.nuance: Govindan, the bride's father and Civakan's uncle, is the mountain; the wedding is that of cousins and the sacrificial hall is the bride's place of marriage.
2460.event: Govindan's daughter is brought to the sacrificial hall to be given to Civakan.

2461.reading: The bride, her fish-long eyes opening like flowers and weighed down by her breasts, trembles with shame and hides her smiling face with her hand, like the moon in the sky caught by a serpent.
2461.event: The bride covers her face in shyness.

2462.reading: The verse likens the sacrifice's sound to the sea and says the truth-seers who have crossed the four Vedas sow the paddy of virtue and bring about the world's joy.
2462.nuance: A Jain work describes a Vedic wedding rite without answering it here; the verse leaves open whether the narrator holds the claim or only describes the priests' belief.
2462.event: The marriage priests begin the sacrifice.

claims.claim: sages who have crossed the four Vedas sow virtue and gain earthly joy through the sacrifice

2463.reading: The priests build the altar with fine sand, darbha and three sorts of fuel, adorned with flowers, and set incense in one jewel-bowl and water in another.
2463.event: The priests make the altar and set out the vessels.

2464.reading: They fill a gold vessel with parched rice, set it with the ghee for the god of fire, tie it with darbha and lay out the three gold-ringed bars and two pure sticks.
2464.event: The priests lay out the offerings.

2465.reading: By the rule of the mantras they take darbha, purify the ghee with it three times, remove it and place it, thinking it over, in the fire-bed.
2465.event: The priests consecrate the ghee and place it on the fire.

2466.reading: As the spoon pours ghee on the eight-finger sticks and the quarters bless, the fire god is said to rise turning right, that fortune may play across the whole sea-ringed land.
2466.nuance: The words 'they say' (என்ப) mark the omen as hearsay; the verse does not endorse the rite.
2466.event: The fire rises on the pouring of the ghee.

claims.claim: a fire that rises turning right when ghee is poured foretells fortune for the land

2467.reading: With gold pot water in the shape of the sea and Jupiter showing, drums, conches and kings roaring, Civakan, king of kings, takes the water into his palm.
2467.nuance: The pouring of water into the groom's palm is the sign of giving the bride; the verse does not name the giver, taken as Govindan.
2467.event: Civakan receives the gift-water that gives him the bride.

2468.reading: As the serpent lets go the moon, Civakan takes the bangled hand of the lotus-faced bride in his left, goes round the fire, and mounts the gold bed.
2468.event: Civakan takes the bride's hand, circles the fire and sits her on the couch.

2469.reading: After the star Arundhati is shown, her feet are washed with milk; he sits looking at the ceremonial offering, like a fanged tiger beside a peahen.
2469.nuance: The word அயினி and the person who washes the feet are obscure, so which rites are meant here is not certain.
2469.event: The couple are shown Arundhati and Civakan sits down with her.

2470.reading: The maids arrange the fifteen things named for the bed, among them a pearl canopy, garlands, swan down and soft cotton, with scented smoke filling the room.
2470.event: The women prepare the bridal bed.

2471.reading: The slim women put the bed's coverings of cool soft cotton and down, hang a curtain, and draw it.
2471.event: The women dress the bed and draw the curtain.

2472.reading: The girls, whose eyes are like two drawn spears, set gem-eared lamps and silver-gold mirrors on both sides of the bed.
2472.nuance: The words மணிச்செவி and படியகம் are rare; the objects are read as vessels and mirrors but are not certain.
2472.event: The women set out lamps and mirrors by the bed.

2473.reading: The women prepare a pleasurable mix of the soft, ripe, red-sap and tender cool-water fruits with sweet honey.
2473.event: The women prepare the mixed fruit and betel items.

2474.reading: They add the scented lime, the bitter white leaf, and the cool liquid scents that give the breath a sweet smell, in gold, gem and coral caskets filled with powder.
2474.event: The women stock the caskets with betel and scent.

2475.reading: The long-eyed girls carry in caskets of musk, vessels of scent, a conch casket of fine cloth, like the creeper of desire growing in the water of love.
2475.event: The women bring in the caskets of scent and cloth.

2476.reading: Civakan the great cloud lets fall a rain of desire, with pearl strings for lightning and the garland for a rainbow, which fills the tank of the bride's heart, and her kohl runs as mud when the sluices open.
2476.nuance: The consummation is told wholly by the figure of a rain-cloud filling a tank; no act is described.
2476.event: Civakan and the bride come together.

2477.reading: After the bride's close embrace, her cloth dishevelled, breasts reddened, her bee-humming wreath crushed by her husband's garland, she is left like a creeper wilted by the flower-plucking.
2477.event: The bride, after the night, lies drained.

links.note: Verse 26 in the opening summary has Civakan winning the nectar-like beauty of his maternal uncle's daughter; 2460 brings that daughter, from Govindan's mountain, to the sacrificial hall to be given.
links.teaches: The poem's opening promise of this marriage is kept here with Vedic rite and a king's gift-water, so the reader sees the match as one planned from the start with the uncle's daughter given by her father's house.

links.note: Verse 29 says Civakan will no longer want the pleasure of women; 2477 shows the pleasure he had in marriage in its fullest.
links.teaches: The full wedding night shows what the hero gave up at the end, so his later renunciation of pleasure counts for more than a hero who never knew it.

links.note: In Kural 1146 the woman says gossip spread like the serpent seizing the moon after one sight of him; in 2461 the shy bride's hidden face is the moon in the serpent's grasp.
links.teaches: The same moon-and-serpent figure stands for exposure in the Kural and for modest hiding in the epic, so the figure is a flexible one for a face that is partly seen.

gains.a: The bride's shyness gains a ready sign of what is hidden, a shame that the Kural's woman does not have because her secret is out.
gains.b: The Kural's couplet gains a contrast in which the same image means a lawful, guarded display, not a scandal.

links.note: The wedding verses lay out darbha, sticks and ghee for the fire with care; siddhar 372 lists observances, vows, the Vedas, fire rites and water offerings as among the outward forms the Siddhar puts aside.
links.teaches: A Jain poem makes the fire rite the centre of a happy wedding while the Siddhar counts the same fire rite among forms to be left behind, so what counts as a sacred act depends on whether the aim is a household or release.

gains.a: The rite's careful detail gains a sceptic who judges all such rites as outward.
gains.b: The Siddhar's list gains a case of the rite performed for a wedding, a purpose the Siddhar does not address.

links.note: 2466 reports the fire rising right as an omen of fortune; Tirumanthiram 551 says the way of sacrifice has no way through while the eight-limbed yoga path leads to samadhi.
links.teaches: The epic reads the fire as a sign of worldly fortune, while Tirumular reads the same fire path as a dead end for release, so the same rite is a good for the household and no good for release.

gains.a: The omen of fortune gains a view that the fire gives no release.
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal gains a scene in which the fire's use is worldly luck and not a claim to release.

links.note: In 2467 drums, conches and kings roar as the bridegroom takes the water; Naladiyar 23 says the same wedding drums can sound as funeral drums that very day.
links.teaches: The roar of the wedding drums sets Naladiyar's warning on how soon joy turns, and the epic's later turn to renunciation is its own answer.

gains.a: The wedding's loud joy gains the reminder that it may not last.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a full wedding in which the drums actually sound.

links.note: Kural 1251 says desire's axe breaks the door of restraint barred with shame; 2477 shows the bride's shame giving way within a sanctioned marriage.
links.teaches: The Kural treats the fall of shame as a defeat, while the epic shows it fall inside a rite-bound marriage, so shame is given up here without the loss the Kural fears.

gains.a: The bride's drained state gains a rule against which shame's giving way is not a fault.
gains.b: The Kural's couplet gains a case in which the bar of shame lifts lawfully.

source_issues: Verses 2457 to 2466, 2468 to 2470, 2473, 2474, 2476 and 2477 were printed in eight half-lines and the build joined them into four lines.
2457 and 2469 contain words (உத்தராசங்கம், அயினி) whose sense is not fixed, so the rites they name are not certain.
The bride is named only in the section title; no verse of this run names her.
